subject: history
title: Yalta, Potsdam and the Origins of the Cold War
welcome_lead: Walk into the conference rooms of Crimea and Brandenburg, where the Grand Alliance fractured into superpower rivalry.
meta_desc: History Cold War Adventure 1: Yalta, Potsdam and the early origins of superpower tensions.
final_note: You have studied the conferences that hinged war's end. Many Cold War flashpoints had roots in their unresolved compromises.

concepts.def: Meeting of Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin to plan the post-war world in the Crimea.
Conference of Truman, Stalin and Attlee (after replacing Churchill) finalising post-war arrangements.
US pledge to support free peoples resisting subjugation, marking the policy of containment.
US economic aid programme for European recovery worth around $13 billion.
Term used by Churchill in March 1946 (Fulton, Missouri) to describe the division of Europe.
US strategy formulated by George Kennan to limit the geographical spread of Soviet power.

walkthroughs.body_html: At Yalta the Big Three agreed on Soviet entry into the war against Japan, the United Nations, the division of Germany into occupation zones and 'free elections' in liberated Europe. Disagreements about Poland — its borders and government — already hinted at later tensions.

By Potsdam, Roosevelt was dead, Truman was president, Churchill was replaced mid-conference and the atomic bomb had been successfully tested. The conference confirmed German partition, demilitarisation and denazification but exposed sharp differences over reparations and Eastern European governments.

Churchill's Fulton speech (March 1946), Kennan's 'Long Telegram', the Truman Doctrine, Marshall Plan, Soviet creation of Cominform (1947) and Berlin Blockade (1948-49) hardened the division of Europe. The formation of NATO (April 1949) and the Federal Republic and German Democratic Republic in 1949 institutionalised the split.
